title: How to Get Rich (Slowly, and for Real): What the Evidence Says About Building Wealth
description: The reader asked how to get rich; this course answers with what the evidence supports. It covers the things that reliably build wealth over a lifetime: earning more through skills and career choices, spending less than you earn, letting compound growth work for decades, avoiding expensive debt, and owning low-cost diversified index funds instead of trying to pick winners. It also looks squarely at the get-rich stories (stock tips, trading, crypto, startup fortunes), how often they work out, and how to spot scams. Examples use US accounts and tax rules, and the course is education, not personal financial advice.
objectives: Calculate net worth, savings rate and compound growth, and explain how time, return, contributions and fees each change the result.
Build a monthly budget with a savings target and an emergency fund goal.
Compare debts by APR, compute the interest cost of minimum payments, and rank debts for payoff.
Explain, using SPIVA data and cost arithmetic, why most actively managed funds trail their benchmark index over long periods.
Describe risk, diversification and asset allocation, and choose a stock and bond mix for a goal and time horizon.
Explain how US tax-advantaged accounts (401(k), traditional and Roth IRA, HSA) work, using the current year's IRS limits.
Identify investment fraud warning signs and survivorship bias in success stories.

preface:
You asked how to get rich. Here is the honest answer, and it is better news than it sounds: most people who build real wealth do it in ordinary ways that you can copy. They earn a decent income and grow it, spend less than they earn, avoid expensive debt, and put the difference into low-cost, diversified investments for a long time. Nothing on that list needs luck, a secret or a guru.

What this book will not do is promise you a shortcut. We will look closely at the shortcuts people sell (stock tips, day trading, the next coin, the dropout founder) and ask the question their stories skip: out of everyone who tried, how many won? Some did, and we will say how. We will also learn to recognize the scams that dress up as shortcuts.

Each chapter does the math with you. You will follow three savers who start at different ages and watch what time, fees and debt do to them, and you can move the sliders yourself in the compound-growth explorer. The examples use US accounts and taxes, and every rule that changes each year comes with its date. This is education, not advice about your own money; by the end you will know enough to make your own decisions, and to know when to ask a professional.

bible.teacher: Dr. Professor teaches this book as an economist who teaches personal finance from evidence: index-fund cost arithmetic (Bogle), research on market efficiency (Malkiel), SPIVA scorecards, regulators' guidance (SEC, FINRA, CFPB, IRS), and behavioral finance, with every number dated and every calculation shown.
bible.promise: By the last page you will know how wealth is actually built, be able to run the numbers on saving, debt and investing yourself, choose low-cost diversified investments with your eyes open, and recognize a scam or a survivorship story when you see one.
threads: The wealth equation: earn, spend less than you earn, invest the gap, and give it time.
Control what you can: costs, taxes, debt and your own behavior; returns are not yours to control.
Possible versus likely: every get-rich route is judged by its base rate, not its best story.
Show the math: every claim about growth, debt or fees comes with a worked calculation.
Education, not advice: general principles, no specific securities, and clear signs for when to see a professional.

runningExamples.name: Three savers: Ana, Ben and Cal
runningExamples.use: Hypothetical people who start saving at 25, 35 and 45 with different savings rates, fees and debts; used for compound growth, debt payoff, fees and account choices.

runningExamples.name: The compound-growth explorer
runningExamples.use: Sliders for starting amount, monthly contribution, annual return, years and annual fee, used from Chapter 3 on; results cross-checked with Investor.gov's Compound Interest Calculator.

runningExamples.name: The reader's own numbers
runningExamples.use: Optional and private: a net worth sheet, budget and debt list the reader builds in Chapters 1 to 4 and reuses later. Sample numbers are given for readers who prefer not to use their own.

runningExamples.name: A get-rich pitch
runningExamples.use: A typical pitch (a trading course, a new coin, a dropout founder's story) taken apart in Chapter 8 for survivorship bias, base rates and scam warning signs.

conventions: US dollars, US accounts, taxes and agencies (IRS, SEC, FINRA, CFPB), stated as US-specific; readers elsewhere are told to look up local equivalents.
Date every number that changes (contribution limits, tax brackets, SPIVA results, interest rates) with its year and source.
Use real (after-inflation) returns for long projections and say which rate is used; never promise a return.
Never name a specific stock, fund, crypto asset or company as something to buy; use fund types and hypothetical numbers.
Mark popular books (Housel; Stanley and Danko) as popular and state the limits of their evidence.
Show every calculation step with units (dollars, percent per year).

canon.cite: Bogle, J. C. (2017). The little book of common sense investing: The only way to guarantee your fair share of stock market returns (10th anniversary ed.). Wiley.
canon.role: The case for low-cost broad index funds: the cost-matters arithmetic and long-run returns, plus chapters on asset allocation and retirement; Chapters 3, 5 and 6.

canon.cite: Malkiel, B. G. (2023). A random walk down Wall Street (13th ed., 50th anniversary ed.). W. W. Norton.
canon.role: Standard account of market efficiency, the evidence on active management, bubbles from tulips to crypto, and a life-cycle guide to asset allocation; Chapters 5 and 6.

canon.cite: S&P Dow Jones Indices. (2026). SPIVA U.S. scorecard: Year-end 2025. S&P Global.
canon.role: Primary data on how actively managed US funds compare with their benchmarks over 1 to 20 years; Chapter 5. Writers use the latest scorecard and quote its exact figures.

canon.cite: Housel, M. (2020). The psychology of money: Timeless lessons on wealth, greed, and happiness. Harriman House.
canon.role: Popular book, not research: behavior, enough, room for error, luck and risk, and patience; Chapters 2 and 6, labeled as popular.

canon.cite: Stanley, T. J., & Danko, W. D. (1996). The millionaire next door: The surprising secrets of America's wealthy. Longstreet Press.
canon.role: Popular book based on 1990s surveys of US millionaires: frugality and the gap between income and net worth; Chapter 1, with its limits stated (survey sample, era, survivorship).

canon.role: Official investor education: the Compound Interest Calculator and Rule of 72 (Chapter 3), fees and fund basics (Chapter 5), and fraud warning signs (Chapter 8).

bible.care: Education, not personal financial advice: teach principles and arithmetic, never recommend a specific stock, fund, crypto asset or adviser, and say when to consult the IRS or a qualified fee-only professional. US-focused: accounts, tax rules and agencies are American, and limits and brackets change every year, so give the year and point to IRS.gov. State the safe rules plainly in the relevant chapters: keep an emergency fund and pay off high-interest debt before investing; no investment is risk-free; anyone promising guaranteed high returns is a warning sign; check sellers on FINRA BrokerCheck and the SEC's adviser search; never send money to someone met online or by message who offers investments; most people in multilevel marketing schemes earn little or lose money. Treat get-rich stories fairly and without mockery: some people do become rich through business, equity and investing, and the book says how, alongside the base rates.
